summary: Defines a MIB module for measuring application performance as end users experience it. It provides objects for network management protocols to report such measurements, in the style of the RMON family. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a scoreboard that tracks how fast a program feels to the person using it, so network managers can spot slow spots.

subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for measuring how available and how responsive applications feel to the people using them.

tldr.problem: Network and server statistics say little about what an end user actually experiences. Users notice only two things about an application: whether it is available and how responsive it is.
tldr.mechanism: The APM MIB defines SNMP objects that record each user transaction as a success or failure plus a responsiveness figure, then aggregate transactions into periodic reports, show recent transactions, and raise notifications when thresholds are crossed.
tldr.outcome: It extends the RMON family with an end-user view of application performance. It is a Proposed Standard and the RFC metadata shows no replacement.

today: RFC 3729 is a Proposed Standard from March 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Measuring What Users Feel
sections.content:
RFC 3729 defines the Application Performance Measurement (APM) MIB, a module for use with network management protocols such as SNMP. It continues the architecture of the RMON MIB by analysing application performance as experienced by end-users. Measuring from the user's side gives a true end-to-end view that combines the application, the desktop, the network and the server, including how they interact.

The RFC argues that, despite all the ways networks and systems can be measured, people perceive only two things about an application. Availability is the percentage of time the application is ready to give service. Responsiveness is the speed at which it delivers the requested service.

The module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580), and its identity sits under the RMON subtree as { rmon 23 }. See RFC 2578 for the data definition language.
sections.plainLanguage: People using a program only care about two things: does it work, and is it quick? This document gives managers a standard way to count both.

sections.title: Transactions and Responsiveness Types
sections.content:
The fundamental item measured is the transaction: an action started by a user that starts and completes a distributed processing function. It begins when the user asks for service (for example pushing a submit button) and ends when the work is done. A failed transaction is one that does not give the user the requested service, whether the cause is processing or transport.

An application protocol may have several commands, called verbs (the RFC's example is POP3 Login and POP3 Retrieval). The MIB can measure the parent application, its verbs, or both, so an operator can watch the top level and drill down to the verbs when trouble appears. Each verb is registered in the Protocol Directory as a child of its application.

Availability is measured the same way for every application, but the responsiveness metric depends on one of three transaction types:

  • Transaction-oriented: fairly constant work per transaction. The metric is application response time in milliseconds.
  • Throughput-oriented: workload varies with the amount of data. The metric is kilobits per second.
  • Streaming-oriented: data arrives at a constant metered rate. The metric is the ratio of degraded or interrupted time to total service time, in parts per million.
sections.plainLanguage: Some jobs are like asking a question and waiting for the answer, some are like downloading a big file, and some are like watching a video. Each one gets its own kind of score, such as how long it took, how fast it went, or how often it stuttered.

sections.title: Aggregating Transactions into Reports
sections.content:
Every transaction is identified by its application, server and client, and carries a success flag and a responsiveness value. Raw transactions are rolled up over a period into statistics. Aggregation always yields a transaction count, a count of successful transactions, and the mean, minimum and maximum responsiveness of the successful ones. It also yields counts for 7 buckets, a histogram whose boundaries are set per application in the apmAppDirTable because applications perform so differently.

There are four aggregation types, from least to most aggregated: flows(1) groups by application, server and client; clients(2) by application and client; servers(3) by application and server; and applications(4) by application alone. Data from different applications is never summarised together, because their performance characteristics and responsiveness metrics can differ so much that the statistics would be meaningless.

A report is configured through apmReportControlTable, which sets the aggregation type, the interval, and how many reports to keep. The interval is in seconds with a default of 3600. Reports should not drift: if there is a fixed processing delay between reports, it should be deducted from the interval.

The RFC also asks that a long-running transaction not be classed as a failure too early. Measurement software should wait as long as the client application itself would wait.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a teacher who writes down every student's quiz time, then makes a summary: one per student, one per quiz, or one for the whole class. This is the same idea, and it never mixes apples with oranges.

sections.title: Groups and Tables of the MIB
sections.content:
The objects are arranged in six groups, which are the basic unit of conformance: if an agent implements a group, it must implement all objects in that group.

  • Application Directory: apmAppDirTable holds a record for each application or verb monitored, including whether it is measured (on or off) and the bucket boundaries.
  • User Defined Applications: apmHttpFilterTable and apmUserDefinedAppTable cover applications not registered in the protocol directory, such as custom in-house ones.
  • Report: apmReportControlTable and apmReportTable for regular aggregated reports.
  • Transaction: apmTransactionTable shows transactions in progress and recently ended ones.
  • Exception: apmExceptionTable sets thresholds that trigger immediate notifications.
  • Notification: two notifications, apmTransactionResponsivenessAlarm and apmTransactionUnsuccessfulAlarm.

Entries in the directory are keyed by an application local index and a responsiveness type, so one application can appear more than once if the agent measures more than one type. HTTP can be targeted by URL: a filter entry matches a path using exact(1), stripTrailingSlash(2) or prefix(3). Two switches shape HTTP results: apmHttpIgnoreUnregisteredURLs limits measurement to URLs that match a filter, and apmHttp4xxIsFailure treats responses in the 400 through 499 range as unavailable.

The transaction table is useful for watching long-lived transactions, since reports and exceptions only act on finished ones. But it is a poor way to collect every transaction, because entries can exist only briefly.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is like a set of labelled notebooks: one lists the programs being watched, one holds the summaries, one lists what is happening right now, and one holds the alarm settings.

sections.title: Exceptions, Caching and the Push Model
sections.content:
The RFC does not require a particular way of measuring. Probe-based, client-based and synthetic-transaction methods are all acceptable, as long as the collected data match the semantics described and the method can measure response time, throughput, streaming responsiveness and availability.

For exceptions, apmExceptionTable sets a responsiveness threshold with a comparison of greater(2) or less(3), and can also flag unsuccessful transactions. Throughput figures can swing wildly for very short transfers, so apmThroughputExceptionMinTime (default 10 seconds) sets how long a throughput transaction must run before it can raise an exception. apmNotificationMaxRate limits notifications to a maximum in any 60 second period, with a default of 1.

Two approaches help when agents are spread across many desktops. With application directory caching, the single object apmAppDirID identifies a well-known registered directory configuration, so a manager that recognises the value need not download the directory again. With the push model, agents send data in notifications instead of waiting to be polled. This suits desktops, which often have changing addresses, are frequently unavailable, and may be laptops that are only sporadically connected.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a boss phoning every desk to ask how things are going, each desk can send in its own update, and it only rings the alarm if something is really wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write and read-create objects can be sensitive, and SET operations without protection can harm network operations. Most of them can be used to make an agent reveal network addresses, application usage and conversation statistics. Even readable objects may be sensitive, so access to GET and NOTIFY should be controlled, and values may need encrypting in transit.

The module contains addresses, machine names, user names and application usage data, which should be treated as sensitive. Administrators should restrict read access to authorised parties, and where read access cannot be restricted, the data should not be gathered. Timing measurements could also help an attacker mount timing attacks against secrets.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It RECOMMENDS considering SNMPv3 security including its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying pre-SNMPv3 versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The scoreboard shows who used what and when, so it should only be shown to people who are allowed to see it, and kept behind a locked door.
